title: Love and limits
hook: Chesed and Gevurah: giving freely, and holding back

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crown: the will above thought, then wisdom's flash and understanding's unfolding. Your line was the flash and the unfolding. Did an idea get a few quiet minutes before you acted? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

A river with no banks isn't a river. It's a flood. It goes everywhere, soaks everything, and reaches nothing in particular. A river that's all banks and no water is just a ditch. What makes a river is both: the water that wants to pour out, and the edges that give it a direction. Parents know this one. So do good friends, and good teachers. Give with no limit and the gift drowns the person. Hold back with no love and the limit turns cruel. Below the top three lights, the map splits into a pair like that. Today, the first of them.
screen: `NO BANKS: A FLOOD.` → `ALL BANKS: A DITCH.` → `A RIVER NEEDS BOTH.`

segments.voice: Chesed. Love, kindness, giving freely. And its partner, Gevurah, strength, restraint, holding back. Turn them four ways. First, where they sit. On the kabbalists' map, Chesed is on the right and Gevurah on the left, like two arms. One reaches out. One holds firm. Second, the faces kabbalists give them. Chesed is linked to Abraham, whose tent in Genesis is open, who runs to feed three strangers in the heat of the day. The prophet Micah closes his book saying God will perform "the mercy to Abraham", and in Hebrew that mercy is chesed. Gevurah is linked to Isaac, the son who was bound on the altar and lived. Jacob, in Genesis, even calls God "the fear of Isaac". Kindness and awe, two fathers, two sides. Third, the images. Kabbalists pair Chesed with water, which flows to whatever is lowest, and Gevurah with fire, which burns away and draws lines. Water alone floods. Fire alone scorches. Fourth, the surprise. Gevurah isn't the villain. Limits are a kind of care. A parent who says not tonight, a friend who says I won't help you do that, a teacher who returns your work marked up: that's Gevurah, and it can be loving. Some teachers say even the making of the world needed both: love to give, and limits to give it shape. Neither side is meant to win. Too much of either, kabbalists say, and the world tips over. Tomorrow, the light that holds them together.
screen: `TWO ARMS: ONE REACHES, ONE HOLDS.` · `ABRAHAM'S TENT, ISAAC'S AWE.` · `WATER AND FIRE.` · `LIMITS ARE A KIND OF CARE.` · then, large: `LOVE AND LIMITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: balance giving and limits today. Settle, and breathe. Let your right hand rest open on your knee, palm up. Think of one place in your life where you give, and maybe give too much, until it floods. Stay with it for a few breaths. Now let your left hand close gently. Think of one place where you hold back, and maybe hold too hard, until it burns. Stay with that, too. Then rest both hands still. Ask, without judging yourself, which one today needs a little more of the other. The bell holds the time.
Chesed. Love and kindness, giving freely: the right arm of the sefirot, linked to Abraham and to water, held in balance by Gevurah, strength and restraint. Today's word.
Your line: love and limits. Today, in one conversation, notice which one you're reaching for, and add a little of the other. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers often speak of acts of chesed, loving-kindness, such as visiting the sick and feeding guests; in Kabbalah and Hasidic thought, Chesed and Gevurah are taught as a pair of qualities a person learns to balance.
